description: We are TERRAVANCE, a team that loves exploring new technologies and working on ideas that can make a difference. Through our project JalDrishti, we are using NISAR satellite data and AI to understand and monitor floods. We enjoy learning, building, and sharing ideas, and are always open to connecting with people who share similar interests.
summary:
We, Team TERRAVANCE, developed a flood Intelligence model and platform which turns NISAR data into flood maps anyone can understand. We have mapped three real 2026 floods - The Assam Monsoon Floods which hit our North-eastern friends gravely, Thailand's Chao Phraya floods and Our Native Chennai's Monsoon Live Tracking while also enabling mapping any region of choice to see extent of flood.
One of our primary goals was to have flood maps that are confident about their accuracy, knowing well that not all dark pixels mean flood (they can be any type of surface or water), and that don't rely only on the basic physics of SAR to map flood. Hence, we built a hybrid, scientifically validated ML model trained on NISAR observations, checked against Sentinel-2 optical labels it never saw, and ran null tests to count false alarms. Comparing NISAR and Sentinel-1 on the same day also gave us one of our biggest findings: L-Band NISAR saw things C-Band Sentinel-1 missed. Other goals of us included having a live tracking of flood changes in regions (especially for our Hometown Chennai which is prone to floods), An "Earth-healing" pipeline tracking how long a land stayed flooded, what dried and what flooded again with impact layers counting residents, cropland, roads and districts inside the flood for Researchers. Finally topping it with 3 modes (Beginner; Intermediate; Advanced) and guided tours to serve people from our NGOs, residents, teachers to researchers and disaster responders.
details:
For every NISAR pass, JalDrishti streams only the area of interest from NASA's ASF DAAC, compares it with dry-season reference passes, and sorts each 20 m pixel into confident flood, possible flood, permanent water or dry. On top of it sit the people, cropland, roads and districts inside the flood, a recovery timeline and a live monitor.

The heart/CORE: A model we can actually trust

From day one, our main question was not "can we make a flood map?" but "how do we know the map is right?" Not every dark radar pixel is flood: it can be a smooth road, sand, a radar shadow or a lake that is always there. So we didn't want a map that relies only on the basic physics of SAR (a dark pixel means water). We also didn't want a black-box ML model that looks good only on the data it was trained on.

Selection of our features:- We gave the model 13 features, each with a physical reason:

  • The radar signal itself: HH and HV relative to the scene's own median and darkest 10%. Scene-relative values carry across dates and tracks, where raw decibels drift. -> (Differing tracks should not give different results for the same surface, hence.)
  • Change from the dry-season reference passes: this separates new flood from water that is always there. Averaged over 7×7 and 15×15 pixels, so a single speckle can't fake a flood.
  • Texture: water is smooth, land is rough.
  • The HH−HV ratio: separates water, vegetation and buildings.
  • Terrain: height above the nearest drainage (HAND) and slope from Copernicus GLO-30, because low ground floods first.
  • Background maps: JRC historical water occurrence and ESA WorldCover land cover.

Our training process: leave-one-date-out (LODO). We had three NISAR passes over Assam with a clear-sky Sentinel-2 image on the same or the next day. We trained the LightGBM model on two of them and tested it on the third, which it had never seen. Each time, the held-out pass was a different date or even a different orbit track. Then we rotated so every pass was tested once. A random pixel split would have been easy and dishonest, because neighbouring pixels from the same image leak the answer. LODO asks the real question: does the model work on a new day it has never seen? 95% confidence intervals come from a spatial block bootstrap, again so that neighbouring pixels can't inflate the score.

A Hybrid Model: We fixed five ways of combining ML and physics before seeing any scores, and picked the winner on the held-out passes. It is the ML probability OR'ed with a physics rescue for dark, low-lying pixels (HH < −15 dB and HAND < 10 m). The physics rescue catches flood that ML alone misses.

The results: (honestly reported)

  • Assam: mean IoU 0.79 on held-out passes (0.76–0.82), against 0.78 for ML alone, 0.74 for a fixed −15 dB threshold and 0.60 for Otsu.
  • False-alarm (null) tests: we ran the model on two dates (10 July 2026 against 16 June 2026 reference pass) with no flood between them, which should show nothing. It flagged 5.9 km² out of 13,178 km² mapped. The physics-only version flagged 47.5 km².
  • New country: trained only in Assam, the model scored IoU 0.61 in Thailand, worse than a simple threshold. We recorded that. And then we added one automatically labelled Thailand scene, made from free Sentinel-2 data with no hand labelling, and IoU rose to 0.84, clearly above the threshold's 0.755 (the confidence intervals don't overlap). JalDrishti adapts to a new region from free data alone.
  • Chennai: we fixed the model before seeing any Chennai result and didn't swap it afterwards, even though another version later scored higher on one date. It scored IoU 0.56–0.60. In dense cities, buildings scatter the radar signal and may hide water in between them, which affects mapping accuracy. Here, we flag those probabilities.

Our biggest finding: NISAR vs Sentinel

On 22 July 2026, Sentinel-1 (C-band) passed over Assam just 41 minutes after NISAR (L-band). We ran the same detector on both and scored them against the same Sentinel-2 reference. NISAR found 74% of the open water against Sentinel-1's 55% (IoU 0.645 vs 0.536). NISAR also found 63 km² of flooded cropland that Sentinel-1 missed, while Sentinel-1 alone saw 23 km². L-band's longer wavelength reaches water under the rice canopy. C-band was more conservative, with fewer false alarms, and we show that too.

Beyond one map, one day: The "Earth-healing" pipeline

A flood map shows one day. Our recovery pipeline merges every pass from every track to show:

  • how long each place stayed under water, given as a range (passes are up to 12 days apart, so a single number would be invented);
  • when it dried;
  • where the water came back.

For the days between passes, we blend the nearest passes from any track. This is labelled Modelled, never Observed. We validated it by hiding each pass and predicting it from the others: blending beat copying the nearest pass on 17 of 20 passes (sign test p = 0.0013). We also built a rain-driven hidden Markov model that failed when moved from Assam to Thailand (0 of 7). We report it and didn't deploy it.

Live-Tracking, Automatic fetch Pipeline

A GitHub Actions job checks NASA's catalogue every 3 hours. When a new NISAR pass over Chennai appears, it maps the pass and updates the site, with no one pressing a button. NISAR's Urgent Response product made a flood map possible 10.4 hours after the pass, against 2–16 days for the standard science product. In 2023, during Cyclone Michaung, the ASF archive has no Sentinel-1 pass over central Chennai between 30 Nov and 25 Dec. In 2026, NISAR images the whole city on two tracks, on back-to-back days, every 12 days.

Map Any Region:
Anyone can map a flood anywhere, not only our three events. Before any mapping starts, JalDrishti checks NASA's ASF archive live to see whether NISAR actually passed over the chosen area. Users search for a place or draw a box (25–12,000 km²) and pick a date. The app then checks three things:

  • whether a NISAR pass covered the box within a day of that date;
  • how much of the box that pass covers (it picks the best one);
  • whether the same track has at least 2 earlier "before" passes, at least 6 days earlier, to compare against.

If , it intimates the user directly ("NISAR did not pass over this box within a day of…"). That saves the user from waiting for a map that can't exist. If it's yes, it shows the track, the coverage and an estimated run time, then runs the same validated JalDrishti model in a free Google Colab notebook. The result is dropped back into the app and shown on the map. A season mode also gives recovery for that region.

Benefits and intended impact

Clouds hide floods from optical satellites exactly when people need answers, and NISAR doesn't need clear skies. JalDrishti makes that view usable by everyone:

  • Residents: Beginner mode (in Tamil, with read-aloud) answers "Is my area flooded?"
  • Disaster responders and NGOs: ranked districts, roads under water, and where water is still standing.
  • Farmers: how long each field stayed under water, as evidence for crop-loss claims.
  • Teachers: guided tours that work as ready lessons.
  • Researchers: every number traceable to its NISAR granule, plus the open-source pipeline and notebook to run "Map a Region" anywhere.

Other USPs

  • Explainable maps: click any pixel and see how much each clue (water-like now, dry before, low ground, signal change) pushed the decision.
  • Honest numbers (Transparency in results): people inside the flood are shown as a range (confident flood only, up to including possible flood), never as "affected".
  • Two-satellite comparison: an agreement map shows NISAR and Sentinel-1 side by side.
  • Three modes and guided tours: Beginner, Intermediate and Advanced each have their own tours. Advanced follows one real pixel from the raw radar to the final map.

Factors we considered

  • Real data only: no synthetic floods, and every number links back to its NISAR granule.
  • No cherry-picking: models and rules fixed before testing; held-out dates and tracks; negative results published.
  • Limits we state openly: dense-city flooding, newly flooded rice paddies counted as "new water", and residents inside the flood not being the same as people displaced.
  • Access: works on a phone, free and open source, nothing to install.

Tools we used

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript.
  • Data access: NASA Earthdata, CMR, the ASF DAAC with asf_search and earthaccess, and Microsoft Planetary Computer.
  • Model and processing: LightGBM, rasterio, h5py, GeoPandas, NumPy and SciPy.
  • App: React, Vite, MapLibre GL and three.js.
  • Automation and hosting: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages; Google Colab for Map a Region.
  • Testing: Playwright and pytest.
  • Hardware: everything runs on a CPU. No GPU is needed, so anyone can reproduce it.

Results of a few tests:

(One of our failed NISAR attempts, Valencia, showed a real limit: a flash flood can come and go between passes. The next pass came 4 days late and only at its swath edge.)
